title: The CPU & Datapath
summary: Open up the CPU. See its parts, the wiring between them, and how one instruction actually flows through.

blocks.markdown:
The **datapath** is the wiring inside a CPU that moves data between its parts to run an instruction.

- Main parts: **ALU**, **register file**, **control unit**, **program counter**, **instruction register**.
- **Buses** carry the data and addresses between them.
- The **control unit** decides which parts switch on for each instruction.
- One instruction = one trip through this wiring.

blocks.subTitle: The parts at a glance
blocks.markdown:
The five pieces you'll meet.

| Part | Job |
|---|---|
| ALU | Does the math/logic |
| Register file | Small fast storage |
| Control unit | Steers everything |

Plus the **PC** (next address) and **instruction register** (current instruction). All wired together by buses.

The **ALU (arithmetic logic unit)** is the part of the CPU that does the actual math and logic.

- Arithmetic: add, subtract, multiply.
- Logic: AND, OR, NOT, comparisons (is A bigger than B?).
- It takes two inputs, applies one operation, and outputs a result plus flags (e.g. "result was zero").

Everything else in the CPU exists to feed the ALU the right values.

The **register file** is a small block of very fast storage slots (registers) built right into the CPU.

- Holds values the ALU is actively working with — far faster than reaching out to memory.
- Typically a few dozen registers, each just a few bytes.
- Can usually be read from and written to in the same cycle, feeding the ALU directly.

Two special registers track *where* the CPU is in a program.

- **Program counter (PC)** — holds the memory address of the **next** instruction to fetch.
- **Instruction register (IR)** — holds the instruction just fetched, while it's decoded and run.
- After each instruction, the PC normally advances to the next address — unless a jump or branch changes it.

The **control unit** reads the decoded instruction and generates **control signals** — the on/off switches that tell each part what to do this cycle.

- Example signals: "ALU, add these two"; "register file, write this result"; "memory, read this address."
- It doesn't compute results itself — it directs traffic so the right parts fire in the right order.

A **bus** is a shared set of wires that carries data, addresses, or control signals between parts.

- **Data bus** — carries the actual values being moved.
- **Address bus** — carries which memory location to read or write.
- **Control bus** — carries the control unit's signals.

Buses are shared, so only one thing can drive a bus at a time — the control unit enforces that.

The **clock** is a steady electrical tick that paces every part of the CPU.

- One **clock cycle** is one tick — the smallest unit of CPU time.
- Registers only update on a clock tick, so every part stays in step.
- **Clock speed** (e.g. 3 GHz) is ticks per second — more ticks, more work done, roughly.

- Data flows left to right; the control unit's signals flow top-down into each part.

blocks.subTitle: Fetch
blocks.markdown:
Take one instruction, e.g. "add two register values." First step: **fetch**.

- The PC's address goes out on the address bus to instruction memory.
- The instruction that comes back is loaded into the **instruction register**.
- The PC then advances to point at the next instruction.

blocks.subTitle: Decode and execute
blocks.markdown:
Next, the control unit **decodes** the instruction in the IR and drives the rest.

- It reads which registers are needed and pulls their values from the **register file**.
- It sets control signals telling the **ALU** which operation to run (here, add).
- The ALU computes the result over the data bus.

blocks.subTitle: Writeback
blocks.markdown:
Last step: **writeback** — the result finds a home.

- For an add, the ALU's result is written back into a register in the register file.
- For a load/store instruction, the ALU result is instead used as a memory address, and data moves to or from **data memory**.
- Then the cycle repeats: fetch the next instruction the PC now points to.

Fetch, decode, and execute each take at least one **clock cycle** — so one instruction can cost several cycles.

- Simple CPUs run each instruction fully before starting the next.
- Faster designs overlap stages of different instructions, called **pipelining** — see [pipelining](pipelining).
- Either way, the datapath's parts and wiring stay the same; only the scheduling changes.

Common mix-ups:

- **"The ALU runs the whole instruction."** No — it only does the math step; the control unit and register file do the rest.
- **"Registers and memory are the same thing."** Registers are a handful of slots inside the CPU; memory (RAM) is much larger and slower.
- **"The PC holds the current instruction."** It holds the *address* of the next one; the IR holds the current one.

blocks.subTitle: What does the ALU do
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What does the ALU do?**

The **arithmetic logic unit** performs the actual math and logic operations — add, subtract, AND, OR, comparisons. It takes two input values and a control signal saying which operation to run, and outputs a result.

It's the only part that computes; every other part just gets it the right inputs.

blocks.subTitle: What is the program counter
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the program counter?**

The **PC** is a register that holds the memory address of the *next* instruction to fetch. After each fetch it normally advances by one instruction's size, so execution moves forward automatically.

Jumps and branches work by writing a new address straight into the PC.

blocks.subTitle: Datapath vs control unit
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What's the difference between the datapath and the control unit?**

The **datapath** is the hardware that actually moves and processes data — ALU, register file, buses. The **control unit** doesn't touch the data itself; it just generates the signals that tell the datapath's parts what to do each cycle.

One does the work; the other gives the orders.

blocks.subTitle: What is the register file
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is the register file, and why not just use memory?**

The **register file** is a small set of storage slots built into the CPU itself, holding values the ALU needs right now. It's faster than RAM because it's physically closer and simpler to access — but it only holds a few dozen small values.

Memory holds everything else; registers hold what's in active use.

blocks.subTitle: Why clock speed isn't the whole story
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Does a higher clock speed always mean a faster CPU?**

No. Clock speed sets how many cycles happen per second, but how much *work* one cycle does depends on the datapath design — pipelining, how many instructions overlap, memory delays. Two CPUs at the same clock speed can differ a lot in real performance.

Clock speed is one input to speed, not the whole answer.
